articles.title: BREAKING INVESTIGATION: £50.3m owed by Rochdale Council companies as £19.5m Council Tax shortfall raises scrutiny
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's draft accounts show £50.309m in Upperbanks company loan balances, £2.02m interest added and only £132,000 repaid in 2025/26. We examine the figures, the 2022 decisions and the councillors responsible for oversight.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING INVESTIGATION | ROCHDALE DAILY

Rochdale Borough Council's own draft accounts reveal that three companies behind the Upperbanks development owed it £50.309 million in contractual loans at 31 March 2026. In the preceding financial year, just £132,000 was repaid while £2.020 million in interest accrued, increasing the total balance from £48.262 million.

The figures sit alongside reporting that the borough accumulated a £19.5 million Council Tax collection shortfall over the decade since 2016. These are very different forms of money: Council Tax is revenue for services, while Upperbanks loans finance long-term property assets and are not necessarily due for repayment now. Yet both invite scrutiny of how the authority manages public finances.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council, draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26, note on soft loans, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Roch Valley Radio, 'Council tax shortfall in Rochdale of almost £20m in 10 years', 12 June 2026: https://www.rochvalleyradio.com/news/local-news/council-tax-shortfall-in-rochdale-of-almost-20m-in-10-years/

WHAT IS UPPERBANKS AND HOW MUCH IS OWED?

The £60 million Upperbanks scheme, beside Rochdale Riverside, comprises 242 rental apartments and a 146-room Hampton by Hilton hotel. The development received more than £17 million from the Future High Streets Fund and over £3 million from Greater Manchester's Brownfield Development Fund. The hotel opened in September 2023.

The council's soft-loan table shows £33.662 million owed by Rochdale BTR Ltd on a property loan and £2.045 million in its working-capital borrowing. Rochdale Hotel Holdings Ltd had a £14.270 million property loan and Rochdale Hotel Ltd owed £332,000 in working capital. Together, these total £50.309 million.

The original loan arrangements included payment-holiday periods under which interest accrued and was added to the loans. The council also confirms the lending was provided below market rates in support of its service priorities. That means a growing balance is not, by itself, proof that any company has missed a scheduled payment. The critical missing information is the agreed repayment profile and actual cash returned to the council.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Rochdale Development Agency, Upperbanks project details: https://investinrochdale.co.uk/regeneration/projects/upperbanks

THE £2 MILLION INTEREST QUESTION

The 2025/26 loan schedule lists £2.020 million of accrued interest, £159,000 in new advances and £132,000 in repayments. Net contractual loans increased by £2.047 million. The £2.020 million interest recorded is more than fifteen times that year's total repayments.

However, the same page contains an apparent inconsistency. Its narrative says 'no new advances were made', while the adjoining table shows £159,000 of advances to Rochdale BTR Ltd's working-capital loan. The council should reconcile the entries and specify whether the amount was new cash, a transfer or an accounting classification.

The accounts also put the soft loans at a far lower carrying amount, £22.690 million, because below-market loans are discounted for accounting purposes. The council says the concessionary benefit to its subsidiaries is treated as an additional investment; the value of that investment is stated as £27.3 million. The difference is not a £27 million write-off: it reflects accounting treatment of long-term, below-market lending.

WHAT ABOUT THE RISK OF NON-REPAYMENT?

The council's draft accounts record a £472,000 expected-credit-loss allowance across relevant loans at 31 March 2026, of which £267,000 relates to the hotel companies, £189,000 to Rochdale BTR Ltd and £16,000 to other loans. The allowance increased by a net £37,000 during 2025/26. This is a forward-looking credit-risk provision, not proof that a borrower has defaulted or that £472,000 has been lost.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 89, impairment table: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

ARE THE APARTMENTS AND HOTEL DELIVERING?

According to Rochdale Development Agency's fourth-quarter delivery plan, 155 of the 242 Upperbanks apartments were occupied on 24 March 2026, with eight more reserved. That left 87 unoccupied at the reporting date, although occupancy had improved from earlier in the year. The agency also reported improving hotel occupancy, average room rates and yields. The public report did not supply a complete profit-and-loss or cash-flow analysis establishing whether the companies were meeting their initial business cases.

Source: Rochdale Development Agency 2025/26 Q4 delivery plan: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122466/2025-26%20RDA%20Delivery%20Plan%20Q4%20FINAL.pdf

WHICH COUNCILLORS WERE INVOLVED — AND WHICH PARTIES?

The scheme's corporate and funding decisions were considered under a Labour-controlled Rochdale Council led by Councillor Neil Emmott (Labour). Councillor John Blundell (Labour and Co-operative) held the Economy and Regeneration portfolio in 2022, when the Upperbanks proposals came before Cabinet. Councillor Carol Wardle (Labour) held the Finance and Corporate portfolio then and continues as the Finance and Growth portfolio holder in 2026.

Councillor Daniel Meredith (Labour and Co-operative), now the Cabinet Member for Regeneration and Housing, has a different documented voting history: minutes of the 22 November 2022 Cabinet meeting state that he expressly requested his vote AGAINST the Upperbanks loan agreement be recorded. The minutes do not specify why he objected, and he must not be portrayed as having approved that agreement.

The 2022 decision approved a loan agreement while delegating the detail of its terms and structure to officers in consultation with relevant portfolio holders. The politicians' portfolios identify responsibility for decisions and oversight, but do not individually establish blame for any loss or wrongdoing.

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet meeting of 22 November 2022, item 19: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=51234&Opt=3&PlanId=0

Source: Rochdale Council, May 2026 Cabinet appointments: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=156&MeetingId=7146

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet portfolio responsibilities: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/mgCommitteeDetails.aspx?ID=116

WHY ARE FINANCIAL FORECASTS RESTRICTED?

On 5 February 2026, Cabinet received an Upperbanks trading-company financial update including forecasts compared with the business cases approved in June 2022. The published decision notes that the council is the ultimate parent undertaking and 100% shareholder. But detailed financial enclosures were restricted from public view, leaving the public unable to independently compare the original profitability, occupancy and repayment forecasts with current performance.

Source: Cabinet decision, 5 February 2026: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieDecisionDetails.aspx?AIId=49322

THE COUNCIL TAX COMPARISON — WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW

Roch Valley Radio reported that the £19.5 million figure was a cumulative Council Tax collection shortfall since 2016, drawn from 2024/25 accounts, including about £1.3 million in 2024/25. It is not evidence of a fresh £19.5 million hole in the council's 2026/27 budget, and should not be directly subtracted from or compared with Upperbanks' contractual loan book as though both were immediately available cash.

The comparison does raise a narrower, evidence-based question: how transparent is the council about its own long-term financial commitments, loan repayments and commercial outcomes while it seeks to maximise Council Tax collection?

QUESTIONS REQUIRING ANSWERS

Rochdale Daily is seeking clarity on the contractual repayment timetable, how much loan interest has actually been received in cash, the latest independent valuations of Upperbanks' assets, the trading companies' current profitability, the £159,000 'new advances' discrepancy, and whether a non-confidential comparison with the original 2022 business cases will be released.

Councillor Meredith's recorded vote against the original loan agreement also merits an explanation of his reasons at the time, without assuming those reasons.

Upperbanks has delivered homes and a hotel to the town centre, while published occupancy data show improvement. Neither physical regeneration nor a large outstanding loan balance alone establishes that the scheme has succeeded or failed financially. The public accounts do, however, make a compelling case for clear reporting of when public funds are expected to be repaid and whether the original forecasts are being met.

This investigation is based on the council's DRAFT 2025/26 accounts, which remain subject to audit. Neither the loan balances nor the credit-loss allowances establish unlawful conduct, fraud or improper spending.

articles.title: Rochdale Pioneers Museum to Host Archive Sessions on Local Folklore
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will offer free creative drop-in sessions this weekend, exploring traditional and supernatural tales from the borough's archives.
articles.content_html:
The Rochdale Pioneers Museum will host free creative drop-in sessions this weekend, inviting visitors to explore traditional, unusual, and even supernatural tales from the borough's archives. The sessions, led by Mitch Robinson, aim to uncover hidden stories and records, ranging from folklore to magical narratives.

As part of the 'Open with Care!' initiative, attendees will have the opportunity to engage with archives that often remain stored away, including old books, documents, and letters. The Co-op Heritage Trust encourages anyone interested in storytelling, history, or creativity to participate, particularly families with older children.

The hour-long sessions will take place at 12.30pm and 2pm, with no prior booking required. Participants can expect a creative and thought-provoking experience, perfect for those looking for something unique to do during the spooky season.

This initiative not only highlights the rich history of Rochdale but also fosters community engagement with local heritage. Those interested in uncovering the borough's fascinating past are encouraged to attend.

articles.title: Roadworks Scheduled on Nowell Road, Pershore Road, and Thornham Lane in Middleton from 26 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced roadworks affecting Nowell Road, Pershore Road, and Thornham Lane in Middleton, set to begin on 26 October 2026, with temporary closures and limited access.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Nowell Road and Pershore Road in Middleton on 26 October 2026. The works will involve temporary closures of these roads, although specific details regarding the duration of the closures have not yet been provided.

In addition to the closures on Nowell Road and Pershore Road, roadworks will also take place on Thornham Lane starting from the same date. These works are scheduled to occur daily from 9am to 4pm, running from Monday, 26 October to Friday, 30 October 2026. The closure on Thornham Lane will extend from the junction with Rochdale Road for approximately 23 metres in an easterly direction, with no alternative route available for vehicles during this period.

Access will be maintained for residents and emergency services where it is safe to do so. The council advises motorists to plan their journeys accordingly and to expect delays in the area due to the roadworks.

For further information, residents can view a map of the roadworks across Greater Manchester on the Rochdale Borough Council website. Details regarding the specific timings and any potential impacts on local traffic will be updated as the work progresses.

articles.title: Bus Services Suspended Between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold Following Collision
articles.excerpt: A road traffic collision at Westwood has led to the suspension of bus services between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold, with ticket acceptance in place on multiple routes.
articles.content_html:
A road traffic collision at Westwood has resulted in the suspension of bus services between Rochdale Town Centre and Freehold. The incident has disrupted travel for many commuters.

In response to the disruption, Transport for Greater Manchester (TfGM) has implemented ticket acceptance on several bus services. Affected routes include the 17, 57, 59, 76, 76A, 81, 83, 84, 114, 149, 181, 182, 409, 411, 435, 436, and 471.

Passengers are advised to check the TfGM travel alerts page for updates on the situation and any changes to service availability. The collision has caused significant delays, and it is currently unclear when normal service will resume.

Local residents and commuters may experience longer journey times due to the disruption. TfGM is working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to Implement New Planning Decision Guidelines from October 31
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council is set to adopt new planning decision guidelines mandated by the Government, which will change how planning applications are processed across the borough starting October 31.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is preparing to implement significant changes to the way planning applications are decided, following new Government guidance. These changes will take effect on October 31, 2026, as mandated by the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026.

The new regulations aim to streamline the planning process by allowing planning officers to determine a greater number of applications. This shift is intended to enable planning committees to focus on larger applications and more complex issues. Under the new guidelines, certain applications will be designated for officer determination and will not be presented to the committee unless referred by a nominated councillor and a council officer.

Additionally, ward councillors will no longer have the ability to automatically call-in applications for committee consideration, nor will there be a threshold for objections that would trigger such a review. This is expected to provide greater clarity and consistency in the decision-making process, according to a report prepared for the council.

On Thursday, Rochdale Council will be asked to formally adopt these changes. Members of the council will still be able to engage with the planning process, raise concerns from residents, and submit material planning reasons, although a member request will not automatically necessitate committee determination.

From October 31, all councils must comply with new Government guidance required by the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026. The aim is for planning officers to determine more applications, allowing planning committees to focus on larger applications and issues. One of the biggest changes is the designation of applications that must be determined by officers and cannot go before the committee. Applications that can be considered by the committee must be referred to it by a nominated councillor and council officer. And applications can no longer be automatically called-in by ward councillors, nor will there be a threshold for the number of objections received that will trigger a committee consideration. On Thursday, Rochdale Council is being asked to adopt the changes. A report to the council said: “The Government’s aim is to provide greater clarity and consistency regarding the role of planning committees in decision-making, so that committees focus on key proposals that matter to an area while more minor and technical decisions are made by planning officers. “Members may continue to engage with the planning process, raise residents’ concerns and submit material planning reasons. A member request will not itself require committee determination, but may be considered by the nominated member and nominated officer.” READ MORE: Flagship training centre reaches construction milestone The changes will see the introduction of two category schedules which set out which applications must be determined by officers and which can be decided by the planning committee. Only planning officers can determine applications under Schedule One which includes householder, minor commercial and minor residential applications, lawful development certificates, non-material amendments and other specified technical applications. Applications which fall under Schedule Two and can be referred to the planning committee include larger planning applications, listed building consent, advertisement consent, consent under a tree preservation order and legal agreements with developers. The starting point is that these must be determined by officers unless the nominated member (planning committee chairperson) and the nominated officer (Director of Economy and Place) agree that the application should be referred to committee. In order for an application to be referred, it must raise “economic, social or environmental significance to the local area, as well as those with significant planning matters relating to the development plan and any other material considerations”. Where the nominated member and nominated officer do not agree, the new guidance states that the application must be determined by an officer. Applications made by or on behalf of the council, a councillor or an officer, including those with which they man have an interest in, can be referred to the planning committee. The report concludes: “If the planning committee determines an application which the regulations require to be determined by an officer, the decision may be subject to judicial review and may be quashed.” SUPPORT THE ROCHDALE TIMES: FOLLOW US ON FACEBOOK Got a story? articles.title: Man Injured in Altercation on Rochdale Road, Middleton
articles.excerpt: A man sustained injuries during an altercation on Rochdale Road in Middleton on October 11, prompting a response from police and ambulances shortly after the incident.
articles.content_html:
A man was injured during an altercation on Rochdale Road in Middleton on the afternoon of October 11. Greater Manchester Police received reports of a disturbance at approximately 4:30pm and dispatched several police cars and two ambulances to the scene.

Upon arrival, officers located the injured man, whose injuries are not believed to be life-threatening. The exact circumstances surrounding the incident remain unclear as investigations are ongoing, according to a police statement.

The police confirmed that they are working to determine the full details of the incident. No further information regarding potential suspects or the nature of the altercation has been released.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.summary: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.body:
Anyone from Rochdale who’s ever limped away from a small mishap will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” For many locals, cruckle means the particular half‑twist or awkward roll of the foot you can often walk off — not a full sprain but a sudden wobble that makes you wince. This usage is recorded in contemporary perceptual descriptions of Greater Manchester speech and has been listed by residents when describing Rochdale’s spoken character. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

The word itself, however, has deeper roots. Historical dialect lexicography gives us a family of related forms — crookle, crukle, cruggle, krukel — all clustered around meanings such as to bend, make crooked, stoop, huddle or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect sources and Scottish dialect records preserve these cognates, showing the same phonetic shape and similar senses across northern English and Scots varieties. In the Dictionary of the Scots Language you can see cognate entries (kruggle / cruggle / cruckle) used with senses like “to crouch or huddle,” and nineteenth‑century dialect glosses list crookle with senses such as “to make crooked; to bend, twist.” ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd00075099))

How did a general sense of bending or crookedness come to mean the small ankle‑roll in Rochdale? Linguists point to ordinary, well‑attested word‑formation processes. A crook/crook‑ family root (suggesting bending, hooking or crookedness) plus a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending can produce verbs that describe small, repeated, or imitative actions — crook → crookle. Comparable northern and Germanic dialect forms show similar semantic shifts from ‘bend’ or ‘stoop’ toward senses connected with awkward gait or limping; the broader comparative work on Germanic dialect vocabularies helps explain why these forms and meanings sit together. In short, cruckle is linguistically predictable as a local survival and narrowing of an older dialect verb family. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/The_semantic_development_of_words_for_%22walk%2C_run%22_in_the_Germanic_languages_%28IA_semanticdevelopm00ihririch%29.pdf))

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? The short answer is: socially, yes — geographically, not absolutely. Perceptual dialect research carried out in Greater Manchester (2024) collected people’s mental maps and comments about local speech; among the keywords used to evoke Rochdale speech were “broad,” “flat,” “guinnel” and “cruckle,” showing that residents and neighbours associate the word particularly with Rochdale. That kind of folk‑linguistic visibility gives a strong local identity to a word even when related forms appear in older records elsewhere. At the same time, historical dictionaries and place‑name evidence show related spellings and senses across northern England and Scotland, so it would be misleading to claim the sound‑type has never occurred outside the area. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Large projects that collect lived speech and crowd‑sourced dialect entries also help explain how such words persist. When the British Library and other public call‑outs gathered regional words, contributors highlighted locally specific items that researchers had not always recorded in older printed dialect dictionaries; popular reportage of that work singled out “cruckle” as an example of a recognisably local term with onomatopoeic appeal. These crowdsourced attestations, together with formal perceptual surveys, are why small words like cruckle keep turning up in contemporary studies of regional identity. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? Cruckle matters because it shows how vocabulary anchors place: the word’s form and original sense are old and shared across northern dialects, but memory, everyday use and local attitude have made it feel distinctly Rochdale. Linguists view it as a useful data point — for historical contact between Lancashire and Yorkshire varieties, for small‑scale semantic narrowing, and for how people use language to say where they’re from. If you’ve got family pronunciations, old spellings or written examples from letters, keep them — local archives and dialect projects welcome material that helps trace exactly when and where words like cruckle shifted meaning and stuck to a place.

articles.title: Construction Completed on Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre in Kingsway Business Park
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre in Kingsway Business Park has reached a significant construction milestone, marking the completion of the first major development in Atom Valley.
articles.content_html:
Construction work has been completed on the Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) located in Kingsway Business Park, Rochdale. This marks the first major development in the Atom Valley project, which aims to foster economic growth and innovation in the region.

The project commenced last November, with the aim of creating a cutting-edge facility dedicated to materials and manufacturing. On Friday, civic leaders, including Mayor of Rochdale Cllr Faisal Rana, were given a tour of the site and an update on its progress from key figures involved in the project, such as Paul Ormerod, Chair of Atom Valley, and representatives from the University of Manchester and Greater Manchester Combined Authority.

Cllr Rana emphasised the importance of the SMMC, stating that it represents more than just a new building; it signifies investment in the community, job creation, and a commitment to a sustainable future for young people in the area. The centre is part of a broader initiative to position Atom Valley as a leading hub for advanced manufacturing and engineering across Greater Manchester.

With the construction phase now complete, the next steps will involve equipping the centre and preparing for its official opening, which is expected to provide new opportunities for local residents and contribute to the strengthening of the local economy.

articles.title: ‘Really nice’: an editor’s visit to the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily's editor visited the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with her little girl and found kind, efficient staff, a fully available menu and a welcome that earned a child's verdict: ‘really nice’.
articles.content_html:
There are plenty of ways to judge a new coffee shop. You can look at the menu, the speed of the service or whether it manages to make a quick stop feel pleasant. But after visiting the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with my little girl, I found that the most telling review came from her.

“Really nice,” she said of the people working there. Two words, and a rather lovely assessment.

As the editor of Rochdale Daily, I spend a great deal of time looking at what opens, closes and changes across the borough. This time, rather than reporting on a launch, I wanted to experience the place as an ordinary customer — and a parent.

What stood out was the staff. They were kind, welcoming and efficient, handling our visit with the sort of ease that makes all the difference when you have a child alongside you. Good service does not need to be theatrical. Often, it is simply being treated warmly while everything runs as it should.

The full menu was available during our visit, too. There were no disappointing discoveries that something we wanted could not be ordered. It is a simple thing, but it matters: choice is only useful when the items are actually available.

The branch, which opened in August near Rochdale Infirmary and Dunelm, provides both indoor seating and a drive-through. For people visiting the hospital, passing along Whitworth Road or simply looking for a coffee stop, those options are convenient. But convenience alone is not what makes a customer want to return.

Children have an uncomplicated way of measuring an experience. They remember whether somebody was kind. They notice when they are made to feel welcome. My little girl did not care about the branding or the opening ceremony; she cared that the people were, in her words, “really nice”.

This was one family visit, not a claim that every visit will be identical. But the team deserve credit for getting the fundamentals right: kindness, efficiency and a menu we could actually order from.

Sometimes a new business makes its best first impression not through a grand announcement but through the people behind the counter. On our visit to Whitworth Road, Starbucks did exactly that.
